theme: Parables; the storm; the Gerasene; Jairus’s daughter
readingInstruction: Read Mark 4:1-5:43. Jesus teaches in parables, stills a storm, frees a demon-possessed man, and heals two women. It is a chapter of authority over the seed, the sea, the spirits, sickness, and death. Notice the repeated question of faith and fear.
settingTheScene: Jesus sits in a boat by the Sea of Galilee and teaches a large crowd on the shore. Mark records only a few parables, but they are key to the kingdom. Then comes a day of wonders. Jesus crosses the lake with his disciples, and in the span of two chapters demonstrates his authority over nature, demons, disease, and death.
observation: “Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow” (4:3).
“He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (4:9).
“It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth” (4:31).
“Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (4:41).
“Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you” (5:19).
“Little girl, I say to you, arise” (5:41).
interpretation:
The parable of the sower is the first of the parables and a key to the rest. A sower scatters seed on four kinds of ground: the path, rocky ground, thorny ground, and good soil. The seed is the word of God. The first three soils show failures: the word is snatched away, withers without roots, or is choked by worries and riches. The good soil hears, accepts, and bears fruit, thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold. Jesus says the parables are given so that those with ears hear, and those without do not understand. They sift. He then tells of the seed growing secretly and the mustard seed. The kingdom starts small, grows by God’s power, and ends large.

That evening, Jesus says, “Let us go across to the other side.” A great windstorm arises, and the boat is filling with water. Jesus is asleep on a cushion in the stern. The disciples wake him: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” He rebukes the wind and says to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” There is a great calm. He asks, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” And they are filled with great fear and say, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” Their fear of the storm has turned into awe at him.

On the far shore, in Gentile territory, a man lives among the tombs, so possessed that no one can bind him. He is called Legion. Jesus casts the demons into a herd of pigs, and the man is found clothed and in his right mind. The townspeople ask Jesus to leave. The man begs to go with Jesus, but Jesus tells him to go home and tell what the Lord has done. He proclaims it in the Decapolis, ten cities of Gentiles.

Back across the lake, Jairus, a synagogue ruler, begs Jesus to heal his dying daughter. On the way, a woman with a twelve-year flow of blood touches his garment and is healed. Jesus stops and says, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” Then news comes that Jairus’s daughter is dead. Jesus says, “Do not fear, only believe.” He takes her hand and says, “Talitha cumi,” “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” She gets up and walks. Jesus is the Lord of life.
connection: Isaiah 55:10-11 says the word will not return empty. Ezekiel 17:22-24 and Daniel 4:10-12 use the image of a great tree. Psalm 65:7, 89:9, and 107:29 show the LORD stilling the sea. Jonah 1 is another storm and sleeping man. Isaiah 65:4 mentions tombs and swine. Leviticus 15:25-30 describes the uncleanness of the woman’s bleeding. 2 Kings 4 tells of Elisha raising a child. 1 Corinthians 15:26 says the last enemy to be destroyed is death.
application:
Ask which soil you are right now. What thorns might be choking the word in you?

Name a storm you face, and hear Jesus say “Peace! Be still!” to it.

Like the healed man, tell someone what the Lord has done for you this week.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to make your heart good soil.
Tell Jesus about a storm you are in.
Thank him that he is Lord of both.
